opus-5.5.text:
I think "hitting a wall" is the wrong way to describe it. What's actually happening is that pre-training has gotten very expensive to scale at the frontier, and the feedback loop has gotten very slow.

If you look at the history, every big jump in pre-training has come from roughly a hundred-x increase in effective compute. That's partly more chips and bigger data centers, and partly algorithmic improvements that let you get more out of the same hardware. Going from GPT-3 to GPT-4 was that kind of jump. To get the next one, you have to build substantially new infrastructure. That takes years, not months. So from the outside it looks like progress has stalled, because you're waiting for the next generation of clusters to come online.

Inside the labs, people are still finding real improvements: better data, better architectures, better efficiency. Those gains compound, but they're incremental. They don't produce the dramatic step changes people got used to between 2020 and 2023.

The other thing that's changed is that the most exciting frontier has moved to post-training and reasoning, especially reinforcement learning on top of a strong pre-trained model, the o1 style of approach. There you're early on the scaling curve, so a relatively small amount of extra compute gets you large improvements. Rationally, if you're a lab, that's where you'd put your marginal effort right now.

But that doesn't mean pre-training matters less. Reasoning models are built on top of the base model, and a smarter base model makes everything downstream better. So in 2025 I'd expect pre-training to keep improving steadily, mostly through efficiency, with the headline gains coming from RL and test-time compute. Then, as the next generation of very large clusters arrives, you'll see another meaningful pre-training jump. It's not a wall. It's a longer cycle.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the "hitting a wall" framing is a little misleading, and it depends a lot on what you mean by it. If you mean that the naive approach of just scaling up pre-training—more data, more compute, bigger models—is giving you diminishing returns relative to the cost, then yeah, I think that's basically true, and honestly it's been visible for a while. The jump from GPT-3 to GPT-4 was enormous. Getting the next one of those jumps purely from pre-training requires something like a hundred times more compute, and there are real constraints on that: data, energy, how many GPUs you can actually put in one place. So the returns are still there, but you're paying a lot more for each increment.

But I'd say that's not the same as pre-training not mattering. Pre-training is still the thing that gives the model its underlying knowledge and its ability to reason in the first place. Everything else builds on that foundation. What's changed in 2025 is that pre-training is no longer the only lever, and it's probably no longer the most important lever at the margin.

The big shift, which I think people have now internalized, is reasoning and test-time compute. With the o-series models, you take a strong pre-trained base and you let it think for longer, and you train it with reinforcement learning to use that thinking well. And the striking thing about that is the scaling curves for reasoning look a lot like the early pre-training scaling curves did—steep and fairly predictable. So in some sense we got a second scaling law just as the first one was flattening. That's where a lot of the progress is coming from now, and I think there's still quite a bit of headroom there, both in how long models can reason and in what domains you can get good reward signals for.

The other piece that I think is underrated is post-training more generally and the data side. A lot of the quality improvements people experience in models now aren't coming from a bigger base model; they're coming from better data, better RL environments, better evaluation of what "good" actually means for a task. That's less glamorous than a new frontier run, but it compounds.

So my honest view is: pre-training in 2025 is more like a mature technology. You still need to do it well, the labs will still push it, and there will be new big base models. But the frontier of capability is moving to what you do with that base—reasoning, agents, tool use, models that can actually operate over long horizons. If someone says pre-training hit a wall, I'd say, sure, but the field didn't hit a wall. It just found a different direction to climb.

astra-6.text:
I think “hitting a wall” is too strong. Pre-training is still the foundation—you’re giving the model a broad understanding of language, code, and the world. The question is whether scaling that alone will deliver all the improvements we want.

What’s changing is that we have other ways to make progress. Post-training can teach a model to use its capabilities more effectively, and giving it more time to reason at inference can help it solve problems it couldn’t answer immediately. So I’d see 2025 less as the end of pre-training and more as a shift toward a broader approach to scaling. Pre-training matters enormously, but it’s one part of the picture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “hitting a wall” is too strong. Pre-training still gives you the foundation: a broad understanding of language, code, and the world that you can then build on. The question is whether scaling that same recipe gives you the same rate of improvement, at the same cost, that it did before.

What’s changed is that we have other ways to make progress. You can train models to reason, to use tools, and to work through problems over multiple steps. And you can give them more computation at inference time, so they spend more effort on a difficult question.

So I wouldn’t frame it as pre-training versus reasoning. They’re complementary. A stronger pre-trained model gives you a better starting point, and post-training helps turn that capability into useful behavior. Pre-training can remain important even if it becomes a smaller share of where the next improvement comes from.
